sammendrag: Unemployment spells are an inevitable feature of dynamic economies and labor markets exhibiting frictions in labor demand due to economic restructuring across firms, occupations and industries. The full cost of unemployment to the affected workers will not only depend on unemployment incidence per se, but will increase with the duration of unemployment spells, or spells of economic insecurity more generally. Against the analysis of unemployment incidence provided above, the current chapter will thus offer more hi-depth analyses of the duration of unemployment spells in both the U.S. and the West German labor market. That is, the chapter will ask for how long states of joblessness typically last in both economies, and which factors determine the duration of these spells of job search. In addition, the analysis will address the relative importance of alternative exit routes from unemployment — exiting into reemployment, setting up one’s own business, entering training measures or, simply, leaving the labor force at all, and the distribution of exit routes among various groups of unemployed workers. From a perspective on marketable resources of workers, a key interest is in the role of human capital, i.e. labor market experience, education, age, or similar factors in leaving unemployment via any of these possibilities. Also, there is an issue of whether and to which extent there are trade-offs between alternative exit options, and the individual and structural determinants of the latter. Institutionally, the key issue is the role of unemployment benefit provision, and its effects on both unemployment duration and job search behavior. The current chapter intends to provide empirical data on these issues for the United States and West German labor market of the 1980s and 1990s.
tittel: Unemployment duration and reemployment rates: a supply-side perspective
